questions.prompt: Per this course's definition, what is a Configuration Item (CI)?
options: Any component of IT infrastructure, service, or asset whose state, configuration, and relationships need to be tracked in order to deliver and manage services
Any record in ServiceNow that has a reference field pointing to the cmdb_ci table
Any device purchased by the IT department and assigned an asset tag
Any record on a table that extends the task table
questions.explain: Lesson 1 is explicit that the real test for a CI is whether tracking its state, configuration, and relationships matters for managing services -- not whether it's expensive, purchased, or assigned a serial number.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes a work record, not a CI -- an Incident has a cmdb_ci reference field pointing at the CI it's about, but having that pointer doesn't make the Incident itself a CI. The Incident is a task-table record referencing something that exists; it is not the thing that exists.

questions.prompt: In the Harrow Logistics lab, the order database runs on a dedicated database server. Why are the database server and the database instance modeled as two separate CI records (cmdb_ci_server and cmdb_ci_database) instead of one combined record?
options: Each has independently trackable state -- the server can be patched and rebooted without the database instance changing, and the database could be migrated to new hardware without its schema or instance name changing
ServiceNow technically forbids a single CI record from belonging to two subclasses at once
cmdb_ci_database records are not allowed to have an operational_status field
Discovery can only scan one cmdb_ci subclass per scheduled run
questions.explain: Lesson 4 makes this explicit: keeping the server and the database instance as separate CIs is exactly what lets each one's state be tracked accurately and independently -- collapsing them into one record would lose that.

questions.prompt: Match each cmdb_ci subclass to the class-specific fields it adds on top of the base cmdb_ci table.
right: Adds database type, schema, and instance name
Adds CPU count, RAM, disk capacity, OS, and virtualization type
Adds version, vendor, and the business criticality of that specific installation
Adds port count and firmware version
questions.explain: Lesson 2 walks each subclass's added fields: cmdb_ci_server adds CPU/RAM/disk/OS/virtualization, cmdb_ci_appl adds version/vendor/criticality, cmdb_ci_network_gear adds port count/firmware, and cmdb_ci_database adds db type/schema/instance name -- all on top of the shared base fields every CI inherits.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: every real CI subclass in ServiceNow -- cmdb_ci_server, cmdb_ci_appl, cmdb_ci_network_gear, and the rest -- extends one shared base table called ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 2 names cmdb_ci as the base table holding the fields common to every CI type, with dozens of real subclasses extending it rather than each reinventing the same common fields.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about why CMDB data quality is genuinely hard, per this course.
options: Infrastructure changes constantly, so a CI record needs an active update every time something is decommissioned, upgraded, or migrated
Data arrives from multiple sources (manual entry, Discovery, imports, integrations) that can genuinely, legitimately disagree about the same field
Without clear ownership, nobody is positioned to notice when a CI's data has gone stale
Most real-world CMDB implementations that fail do so because of a technical limitation in the ServiceNow platform
Once Discovery is configured and running, CMDB data quality is permanently solved and needs no further governance
questions.explain: Lesson 3 names constant change, conflicting sources, and unclear ownership as the three real reasons data quality is hard. It is explicit that most failures are governance and process failures, not platform limitations, and Chapter 4 reinforces that Discovery feeds the CMDB but never replaces the governance work from Chapter 5 -- so both D and E are false.

questions.prompt: A cmdb_rel_ci record has type "Depends on :: Used by", with an application as the parent and a database server as the child. Read from the database server's (child's) side, what does this relationship say?
options: The database server is used by the application
The database server depends on the application
The database server runs the application
The database server is hosted on the application
questions.explain: Lesson 5 explains the directional pair: the parent (the application) depends on the child; read from the child's side, the child is used by the parent, so the database server's side of this relationship reads "used by the application".

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what the Dependency View actually is?
options: A graphical read of the same cmdb_rel_ci relationship records that already exist -- it doesn't calculate or store anything new
A separate data source that recalculates relationships independently of cmdb_rel_ci
A feature that only works after Service Mapping has been licensed and configured
A report that shows only the CIs that have no relationships at all
questions.explain: Lesson 6 is explicit that the Dependency View isn't a separate data source and doesn't calculate anything new -- it's a graphical read of exactly the relationship data already on cmdb_rel_ci, laid out for a human to follow at a glance.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about manual relationship documentation versus Service Mapping.
options: Manual documentation is simple to set up but requires ongoing human upkeep every time infrastructure changes
Service Mapping discovers relationships automatically by tracing real network and process-level connections
Service Mapping is switched on by default on every ServiceNow instance, with no separate licensing
Most mature ServiceNow instances use only one of the two approaches, never both
Service Mapping can surface relationships nobody had manually documented because nobody fully knew they existed
questions.explain: Lesson 6 describes Service Mapping as a separately available capability, similar in spirit to Performance Analytics or IntegrationHub, that typically requires its own licensing -- so C is false. It also states most mature instances use both approaches for different kinds of relationships, so D is false too.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of tracing transitive impact for a failing database server in the correct order, from the failed CI outward to the real business impact.
items: The database server is found to be used by the Order Processing application server (the direct, one-hop relationship)
The Order Processing application server is found to run the Order Processing application
The Order Processing application is found to support the Online Ordering business service
The correct impact statement is reached: Online Ordering is affected, not just a database server
questions.explain: Lesson 7's worked example walks exactly this chain -- stopping at the first hop would understate the real impact; transitive impact follows each further relationship until it reaches the business service level that actually matters to the people who notice it.

questions.prompt: Match each relationship type pair to the situation it's actually used for.
right: Used for application-to-server, e.g. an application running on a server
Used for VM-to-hypervisor or CI-to-cloud-infrastructure, e.g. a VM hosted on a host
Used for the general case where one CI's availability depends on another's, e.g. an application and the database it needs
questions.explain: Lesson 5 names these as the real, out-of-box pairs: "Runs on :: Runs" for application-to-server, "Hosted on :: Hosts" for VM-to-hypervisor or cloud infrastructure, and "Depends on :: Used by" for the general availability-dependency case where no more specific pair applies.

questions.prompt: Before CSDM existed as a published standard, what real problem did ServiceNow instances actually have, per this course?
options: Each module (ITSM, ITOM, Service Portfolio Management) and each implementation team built its own ad hoc structure for services, applications, and infrastructure, so data shaped for one module often didn't match what another module expected
ServiceNow technically prevented any CI from being related to more than one application
The cmdb_ci base table did not yet support subclassing at all
Discovery could not run on any instance until CSDM was installed
questions.explain: Lesson 9 names this directly: before a standard model, every module had grown its own expectations and every implementation team made its own judgment calls, so a dashboard or report built for one module could misread or fail to find records intended for another.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a service defined by the business outcome it provides (e.g. "Payroll", "Email") rather than by the technology underneath it is called a ________ Service in CSDM.
questions.explain: Lesson 11 defines a Business Service as a service from the business or customer's point of view, defined by the outcome it provides, not by the technology underneath it.

questions.prompt: "Payroll" is a Business Service. Which of these is the most plausible Technical Service it would depend on?
options: The payroll processing application stack -- the payroll application, its database, and the servers running them
A specific hardware serial number on one server
The named individual who owns the Business Service record
The Discovery Schedule that scans the payroll server's subnet
questions.explain: Lesson 11 describes the dependency chain: a Business Service depends on one or more Technical Services, which are built from real CIs -- the Technical Service is the technical capability (an application stack), not a hardware attribute, an owner, or a schedule record.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a phased CSDM rollout in the correct top-down order, per this course's recommended approach.
items: Identify and document the organization's most critical Business Services, judged by revenue impact, customer visibility, and regulatory exposure
Identify the Technical Services that actually deliver each priority Business Service
Document the specific CIs -- servers, databases, application instances -- that make up each Technical Service
questions.explain: Lesson 12 argues for top-down phasing precisely so every CI documented already has a reason to exist in the model, instead of cataloging infrastructure first and hoping service context gets added later.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about CSDM's layered domain model.
options: The foundational/shared layer holds locations, companies, and core infrastructure CIs that other layers depend on
The design-time/planning layer holds services and applications being proposed or built, but not yet live in production
The live/operational layer is what Incident and Problem management, and impact analysis, should trace through
CSDM recommends storing planning-stage and live production data together in one undifferentiated layer so nothing gets missed
A newly funded but not-yet-deployed application belongs in the live/operational layer
questions.explain: Lesson 10 is explicit that conflating planning and operational data confuses both impact analysis, which should only trace through what's genuinely live, and portfolio planning, which needs to see the pipeline without live production noise -- so a funded-but-undeployed application belongs in the planning layer, not the live layer, and D and E are both false.

questions.prompt: Why can't Discovery scan a customer's internal network directly from the ServiceNow instance, without a MID Server?
options: ServiceNow's instance runs in ServiceNow's own cloud and has no direct line of sight into a customer's internal network, just like any other cloud-hosted integration
Discovery Schedules are technically incapable of running more than once per day
MID Servers are required only for Vertical Discovery, never for Horizontal Discovery
Credential records can only be stored on a MID Server, never referenced by the cloud instance
questions.explain: Lesson 14 ties this directly back to Course 7's MID Server material: the instance runs in ServiceNow's cloud and cannot directly reach a customer's internal network, so a MID Server sitting inside that network is what actually sends probes and relays results back, for any kind of Discovery.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the record that defines when Discovery runs (e.g. nightly, weekly) and which IP range or network segment it scans is called a Discovery ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 15 defines a Discovery Schedule as exactly this: the record controlling when Discovery runs and what range it scans when it does.

questions.prompt: Match each device type to the credential protocol Discovery typically needs to authenticate against it.
questions.explain: Lesson 17 lists these pairings directly: a Linux server typically needs SSH credentials, a Windows server typically needs WMI credentials, and a network device typically needs SNMP credentials -- one credential doesn't cover every device type because the protocols themselves differ.

questions.prompt: An incident responder needs a precise, complete dependency map for one specific business-critical application during an active outage -- not a general infrastructure inventory. Which approach is the right fit?
options: Vertical Discovery, tracing that one application's full dependency chain end to end
Horizontal Discovery, scanning broadly across every infrastructure type in the environment
A Discovery Schedule configured to run once a year
Manually re-typing every CI field from scratch during the outage
questions.explain: Lesson 16 draws exactly this line: Horizontal Discovery builds broad baseline coverage, while Vertical Discovery goes deep on one specific service's full dependency chain -- precisely what an incident responder needs during an outage.

questions.prompt: Put Discovery's real, phased process in the correct order.
items: An initial ping sweep or port scan checks which IP addresses in the scheduled range have something listening at all
Discovery classifies what kind of device each responding address actually is
Discovery runs only the specific probes appropriate to that device type
questions.explain: Lesson 15 names this exact three-phase order -- scan, classify, probe -- and explains that classifying first is what keeps Discovery from wastefully asking irrelevant questions, like asking a network switch for its installed Windows software.

questions.prompt: Per this course, what does a Reconciliation Rule determine?
options: Which data source's value wins on a specific field when multiple sources report conflicting data for the same CI
Whether two incoming records describe the same real-world asset
Which CI class a given relationship type is allowed to apply to
How often a Discovery Schedule re-scans a given IP range
questions.explain: Lesson 19 defines Reconciliation Rules as deciding, once two records are already confirmed to be the same CI, which source's value wins on a field where sources disagree -- the authoritative-source decision, enforced automatically instead of defaulting to whichever source wrote last.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes what an Identification Rule decides, not a Reconciliation Rule. Identification decides whether two incoming records are the same CI in the first place; Reconciliation only applies after that match is already confirmed, deciding which field value wins. The lesson is explicit that one rule type can be working correctly while the other is still producing wrong data -- they solve genuinely different problems.

questions.prompt: Two CI records are confirmed, after human review, to represent the same physical server. What is the correct cleanup action, and why?
options: Merge them into one surviving CI, so relationships, Incident history, and other references are re-pointed instead of lost
Delete the newer of the two records, since it's the most likely to be the duplicate
Delete the older of the two records, since Discovery's data is always more current
Leave both records in place and just note in a comment that they're duplicates
questions.explain: Lesson 20 is explicit that merging, not deleting, is the correct fix -- deleting a duplicate record deletes every Incident link, relationship, and report history attached to it, with no error raised, while merging consolidates all of that onto the single surviving CI.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the CMDB Health Dashboard's four scored dimensions.
options: Completeness measures whether required fields are actually populated on a CI, with rules defined per CI class
Correctness catches values that are present but nonsensical or out of range, like a CPU count of 0
Compliance measures whether CIs align with the outcomes of Identification and Reconciliation rules
Duplicate rate is folded into the Completeness score rather than scored as its own dimension
A low Completeness score should translate into a specific, bounded remediation task, not a vague "fix the CMDB" instruction
questions.explain: Lesson 18 scores duplicate rate as its own, fourth dimension, separate from Completeness, precisely because duplicates cause a distinct kind of problem -- silently splitting relationships, incidents, and cost data across two records that should be one -- not a completeness problem.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: an attribute reliable enough on its own to prove two records describe the same asset (like a hardware serial number) is called an ________ identifier in an Identification Rule.
questions.explain: Lesson 19 contrasts an independent identifier (reliable alone, like a serial number) with a dependent identifier (only proves a match in combination with another attribute, like Host Name plus Domain).

questions.prompt: A CMDB launches with a clean Health Dashboard score, well-configured Identification and Reconciliation rules, and Discovery running on schedule. One year later, the score has quietly slid back down. What does this course say is the most likely real cause?
options: Nobody was given named, individual ownership of specific Business/Technical Services or CI classes, with a recurring review cadence to catch drift
The ServiceNow platform has a technical limitation that causes CMDB data to decay over time regardless of configuration
Discovery Schedules automatically disable themselves after twelve months
Identification Rules and Reconciliation Rules expire annually and must be recreated from scratch
questions.explain: Lesson 21 names this directly as the real, well-documented reason most CMDB implementations fail: technical configuration alone has no memory and no accountability, and without named ownership and a scheduled review cadence, a correctly built CMDB decays the moment nobody is watching it.

questions.prompt: In the Patient Scheduling capstone, SCHED-SQL-01 (the database instance) goes down for scheduled maintenance. Why does this affect both SCHED-APP-01 and SCHED-APP-02, even though neither server itself is touched by the maintenance?
options: Both app servers have a "Depends on" relationship to SCHED-SQL-01, so the application they run can't function correctly while the database it depends on is offline, even though the servers themselves stay up
SCHED-LB-01 automatically reroutes all traffic to the EHR Integration Service during maintenance windows
SCHED-APP-01 and SCHED-APP-02 each have their own private copy of the database, so maintenance should have no effect on the application
The Patient Scheduling Business Service record is automatically deleted whenever a dependent CI enters maintenance
questions.explain: Lesson 24 documents this exact relationship: SCHED-APP-01 and SCHED-APP-02 both depend on SCHED-SQL-01, so a database outage affects both app servers and the application they run, even though neither server's own configuration changed.

questions.prompt: Match each capstone CI to the cmdb_ci subclass it was built on.
questions.explain: Lesson 24 assigns Patient Scheduling App to cmdb_ci_appl, the two application servers to cmdb_ci_win_server, SCHED-SQL-01 to cmdb_ci_db_instance, and SCHED-LB-01 to cmdb_ci_lb_device.

questions.prompt: Put these capstone phases in the order this course actually sequences them.
items: Scope the Business Service and Technical Service, and draw an explicit boundary around what's out of scope
Build the real CIs and relationships that make up the Technical Service
Map the Technical Service to its Business Service, hand infrastructure CIs off to Discovery, and configure Identification Rules to prevent duplicates
Write the governance plan: named ownership and a recurring review cadence
questions.explain: Lesson 23 lays out this exact order -- scope first, build second, formalize and validate third, govern last -- mirroring how a real CMDB implementation actually gets staffed and sequenced, rather than jumping straight into typing CI records.

questions.prompt: Why does the Patient Scheduling capstone add a single "Sends Data To" relationship to the EHR Integration Service instead of building CI records for the EHR platform's own infrastructure?
options: The EHR platform is already its own Business Service with its own owner and Technical Services modeled elsewhere in the CMDB -- re-modeling it here would be out of this build's scope and risk leaving half-finished records nobody maintains
ServiceNow technically forbids a relationship from crossing between two different Business Services
The EHR platform has no infrastructure that could be modeled as CIs
Discovery already deleted the EHR platform's CIs before this capstone started
questions.explain: Lesson 23 draws this scope boundary explicitly, citing Chapter 1's warning that CMDBs trying to model everything at once end up bloated with half-finished records nobody maintains -- so the capstone adds exactly one relationship to show the handoff, without re-modeling infrastructure it doesn't own.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the capstone's three-frequency governance review cadence.
options: Monthly, the Technical Service Owner reviews the Health Dashboard for this service and follows up on anything that regressed
Quarterly, the Business Service Owner and Technical Service Owner jointly confirm the CSDM mapping still reflects what's actually running
Annually, every CI gets re-certified -- confirmed still needed, still correctly classified, and still correctly related
All three reviews happen on the same monthly schedule, just performed by different people
An orphaned CI (showing no relationships at all) on the dashboard usually means infrastructure was added without being documented
questions.explain: Lesson 26 is explicit that one review frequency isn't enough because different problems surface at different speeds -- monthly for dashboard regressions, quarterly for the CSDM mapping, and annually for full CI re-certification -- so D, which claims they're all on the same schedule, is false.
